title: The sea star experiment
teaches: How one predator can keep many species on a shore, and what a keystone species is

parts.title: Throwing sea stars into the sea

blocks.text: Mukkaw Bay is a small, rocky bay on the Makah Reservation, near the northwestern tip of Washington State, open to the Pacific. At low tide its rocks are crowded: bands of barnacles, beds of blue-black California mussels, goose barnacles in clusters, limpets and chitons grazing the bare patches, anemones, sponges and several kinds of seaweed. Among them, mostly lower down, sit big ochre sea stars, purple or orange, as wide as a dinner plate.

In June 1963 a young zoologist from the University of Washington, Robert Paine, picked a stretch of this shore about eight metres long and two metres from top to bottom. He pried off every ochre sea star he could find with a crowbar and threw it as far out into the bay as he could. He came back every month or two and did it again, for years. Beside it he left a matching stretch alone.

The ochre sea star is the shore's top predator. It eats mussels mostly, along with barnacles, limpets, chitons and snails, prying shells open with its tube feet and pushing its stomach inside to digest them. Remove it, and you might expect all its prey to do better. The question Paine was asking was what happens to everything else.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: From 1963 Robert Paine removed every ochre sea star from a stretch of shore at Mukkaw Bay, Washington, and left a matching stretch alone.
The ochre sea star eats mussels mostly, and barnacles, limpets, chitons and snails.

blocks.text: Within months, acorn barnacles settled thickly on the cleared stretch, covering most of the open rock. Then the mussels and goose barnacles moved in and grew over the acorn barnacles, crushing and smothering them. The seaweeds lost the rock they grew on; the limpets and chitons, with nowhere left to graze, moved off or died. By 1966 the number of species on Paine's stretch had fallen from fifteen to eight. On the stretch left alone, the shore was as varied as ever.

blocks.caption: A stretch of rock as a grid of space, one colour per kind. Mussels spread into bare rock next to them and grow over other kinds; sea stars eat mussels in patches. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then throw out the sea stars and run at least eight years

blocks.text: The thing every animal and alga on that rock needs is space. The California mussel is the best competitor for it: it grows fast, attaches with strong threads, and grows over anything that can't move out of its way. Left alone, it takes almost everything, just as Gause's *P. aurelia* took the whole tube in lesson 6. The sea star is what stops it. By eating mussels, it keeps opening gaps in the beds, and in those gaps barnacles, algae and grazers find room to settle.

Switch off the mussels' ability to overgrow in the figure and removing the sea stars hardly matters. The effect depends on what the predator eats. A predator that mostly ate some weak competitor would make little difference by its absence. This one eats the strongest competitor on the shore, and that is what makes it important.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Without sea stars, mussels took over the rock and species fell from fifteen to eight.
Mussels are the best competitor for space; sea stars, by eating them, keep space open for others.
A predator matters this much when what it eats is the dominant competitor.

blocks.text: In 1969 Paine gave a name to a species like the ochre sea star. In an arch, the **keystone** is the wedge-shaped stone at the top. It carries no more weight than any other, but take it out and the whole arch falls. A **keystone species** is one whose effect on its community is far larger than its numbers would suggest. Sea stars are a small fraction of the animals on a shore; remove them, and its whole make-up changes.

The idea spread far beyond Mukkaw Bay. Ecologists looked for keystones everywhere, and found some: sea otters on kelp coasts (lesson 8), beavers whose dams turn a stream into a chain of ponds, elephants that knock over trees and keep a savanna open, and fig trees that fruit through the lean season when nothing else does. They also learned that most species are not keystones. Take one species of beetle out of a forest and, as far as anyone can measure, very little changes.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A **keystone species** has an effect on its community far larger than its numbers.

blocks.text: Rocky shores everywhere are striped: horizontal bands of barnacles, mussels and seaweeds, each at its own height between high and low tide. A little earlier than Paine, the American ecologist Joseph Connell had used a shore to ask what sets the edges of those bands. On the Isle of Cumbrae, in the Firth of Clyde in Scotland, two barnacles lived one above the other: a small one, *Chthamalus*, high on the rock, and a bigger one, *Balanus*, below it.

Connell mapped every barnacle on patches of rock and followed them for months. He scraped *Balanus* off some patches and left others alone. Where *Balanus* was gone, young *Chthamalus* settled and survived well below their usual band. Where *Balanus* stayed, it grew faster, lifted the little *Chthamalus* off the rock or crushed them, and took their space. The upper edge of each band was set by drying out at low tide, which *Chthamalus* could stand and *Balanus* couldn't. The lower edge of *Chthamalus*'s band was set by competition.

blocks.caption: Connell's two barnacles on a Scottish shore. The upper limit of each is set by drying out; the lower limit of the small one is set by the bigger one crowding it out.

blocks.text: Connell's results, published in 1961, and Paine's together made the shore a model for the whole subject. The physical world sets where a species *can* live. Other species, competing with it and eating it, decide where it *does* live. And because the shore is small, slow and easy to reach at low tide, ideas can be tested there by simply moving things around.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Connell: the upper edge of each barnacle's band is set by drying out; the lower edge of the small barnacle's is set by competition.
Physical conditions set where a species can live; competitors and predators decide where it does.

blocks.text: What Paine and Connell did is called a **removal experiment**. You take one species away from a patch, leave a matching patch alone as a **control**, and watch what changes. It sounds simple, but it was a new way of doing ecology. Before it, most ecologists described what they saw and argued about causes. Removal let them test those causes directly, the way a chemist leaves one ingredient out of a mixture.

The control matters as much as the removal. Shores change from year to year by themselves: a cold winter, a storm, a big settlement of barnacle larvae. Without a matching stretch left alone, Paine couldn't have told the mussels' takeover from an ordinary bad year. Every result in this lesson comes from comparing two patches that differed in one thing.

Paine kept his experiment going for decades, and his students and their students went on to run removal experiments on shores, in streams, lakes and grasslands around the world. When a disease nearly wiped out sea stars along the whole Pacific coast in 2013 and 2014, the shores became an accidental removal experiment on a giant scale.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A **removal experiment** takes a species away from one patch and compares it with a **control** patch left alone.
Without the control, ordinary changes from year to year could be mistaken for an effect.

blocks.caption: Six questions on keystones and shores
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: On another shore, a predatory snail eats mostly a rare, slow-growing limpet. Mussels there are eaten by nothing. What happens if you remove the snail?
choices: Little changes: it doesn't eat the dominant competitor
items.why: A predator's removal matters most when it eats the species that would otherwise take over. A snail eating a rare limpet keeps nothing in check that matters to the rest.

items.ask: Why did the number of species on Paine's stretch fall when he removed the sea stars?
choices: Mussels, no longer eaten, grew over the rock and smothered other kinds
The sea stars had been feeding the other kinds
Without sea stars, the water got colder
items.why: Space is what everything on the rock needs, and the mussel is the best at taking it. Sea stars had kept opening gaps; without them the mussels filled the rock.

items.ask: Connell scraped away the big barnacle Balanus. The small barnacle Chthamalus then lived lower on the rock than before. What does that show?
choices: Competition with Balanus had set Chthamalus's lower limit
items.why: Chthamalus could live lower; it was being crowded out there. So competition, not the physical conditions, set the bottom edge of its band.

items.ask: Why did Paine leave a matching stretch of shore untouched?
choices: So he could tell the effect of removing sea stars from ordinary changes from year to year
To give the sea stars somewhere to live
items.why: A control patch experiences the same weather, storms and larval settlement. Only a difference between the two patches can be put down to the removal.

items.ask: Which of these is the best description of a keystone species?
choices: One whose removal changes its community far more than its numbers would suggest
The most common species in a place
items.why: A keystone's importance is out of proportion to its abundance. Many top predators aren't keystones, and the most common species usually isn't one.

items.ask: Imagine a coast where a disease kills most sea stars. If Paine's results hold there, what would you expect to see in the mussel beds over the next few years?
choices: Mussel beds spreading over open rock
items.why: With their main predator gone, mussels can spread into space that was kept open, as on Paine's cleared stretch.

summary: **Paine removed ochre sea stars from a stretch of Washington shore from 1963.** Within three years its species fell from fifteen to eight.
**Mussels took the space.** The California mussel is the best competitor for rock; without sea stars eating it, it smothered other kinds.
**The predator kept diversity up by eating the dominant competitor.** A predator of a weak competitor wouldn't matter as much.
**A keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers.** Sea stars, sea otters and beavers are examples; most species aren't.
**Connell's barnacles: drying sets the upper edge, competition the lower.** Physical conditions set where a species can live; other species decide where it does.
**Removal experiments test causes.** Take a species away from one patch and compare with a control patch left alone.
